# The Office of Unnecessary Bridges

The bridge arrived on a Thursday, folded into a brown envelope.

Mara found it between a complaint about pigeons and the quarterly invoice for municipal string. The envelope bore no return address, only the words **FOR THE ATTENTION OF WHOEVER STILL CARES**, which technically made it somebody else’s responsibility. Mara had cared quite a lot when she joined the Department of Roads and Crossings twenty-three years earlier, but recently she had been conserving it.

She opened the envelope with a ruler.

Inside was a bridge, approximately six inches long, made of pale stone. Three arches supported a narrow roadway. Along one side stood seven lampposts, each no bigger than an eyelash. A patch of moss grew beneath the middle arch.

There was also a note.

*It belongs on Bellwether Street. You will know where.*

Mara looked out at Bellwether Street.

It contained a bakery, a shuttered cinema, two bus stops, and a man wrestling a rolled carpet into a taxi.

There was nothing to cross.

***

At eleven, she took the bridge to her supervisor.

Mr. Venn was eating a pear with a knife, a practice Mara considered unnecessarily threatening in a person who controlled annual leave.

“Promotional object,” he said.

“It has moss.”

“So do some promotional objects.”

“One of the lamps is on.”

He leaned closer.

The fourth lamppost emitted a warm yellow light. Beneath it, something moved: a person, perhaps, though too small to resolve.

“Electrical,” said Mr. Venn.

“There’s no battery.”

“Solar.”

“It came in an envelope.”

“Residual.”

Mara put the bridge on his desk. A faint breeze passed through the room, carrying the smell of river mud.

Mr. Venn set down his knife.

For a moment, neither spoke.

Then he opened a drawer and removed a blue form.

“Unsolicited infrastructure,” he said. “We haven’t had one in years.”

***

The form required the bridge’s dimensions, composition, likely load-bearing capacity, and reason for existing.

Mara filled in the first two. For the third, she wrote *unclear*. For the fourth, after some consideration, she wrote *crossing*.

Mr. Venn returned it.

“Too general.”

“That’s what bridges are for.”

“That is what authorized bridges are for. We cannot assume.”

By lunchtime, the bridge had grown to the length of her keyboard.

Mara moved her sandwich.

By three, it occupied most of the desk, and water had begun collecting beneath the arches. Not much: a shallow ribbon running over the scratched laminate, disappearing before it reached the edge.

A tiny leaf floated through.

At four, the telephone rang.

“Department of Roads and Crossings.”

“Has it arrived?” asked a woman.

“Who is this?”

“Is the fourth light working?”

“Yes.”

“Oh, good.”

“Did you send us a bridge?”

“Not exactly. I sent it back.”

“Back from where?”

The woman was silent long enough that Mara thought the connection had failed.

“From a place I couldn’t stay,” she said.

Then she hung up.

***

There was a municipal archive beneath the west staircase, in a room the building directory described as Storage B.

Mara knew the archivist, Mr. Ilyan, because he had once helped her locate the original dimensions of a roundabout that had become gradually oval through successive repairs.

He listened without interruption.

Then he said, “Stone or iron?”

“Stone.”

“Number of arches?”

“Three.”

“Any lamps?”

“Seven.”

He stood so suddenly that his chair rolled into a filing cabinet.

“Don’t let them classify it as surplus.”

“Why?”

“They auction surplus.”

From a shelf above the radiator, he retrieved a narrow ledger bound in green cloth. Its spine read **CROSSINGS: NON-GEOGRAPHICAL, 1881–1914**.

Inside were drawings of bridges spanning alleys, bedrooms, market stalls, and, in one alarming case, a dining table.

“Before the reorganization,” he said, “we maintained all sorts.”

“Bridges to where?”

“Not where. Across.”

He turned a page.

The drawing showed Mara’s bridge at full size on Bellwether Street. Beneath it, instead of a river, the artist had drawn an empty rectangle.

A handwritten caption read:

*For distances not measurable by the surveyor.*

***

Mara had been a competent person for most of her life.

At school, she remembered permission slips. At work, she caught errors before they became expensive. When her mother grew ill, she learned the names of medications, the schedules of specialists, and which supermarket sold the soup her mother would still eat.

Competence had carried her through those months and the weeks afterward.

There were calls to make, a flat to clear, and a dispute with the gas company. Her younger brother, Tomas, came on the second weekend. They worked well together until they reached the kitchen.

He wanted their mother’s chipped yellow kettle.

Mara said it was unsafe.

He said he would not use it.

She said there was no point keeping broken things.

He said she had already thrown away everything that mattered.

The argument lasted eighteen minutes. Its consequences had lasted eleven years.

Now they exchanged birthday messages consisting of complete sentences without questions.

Occasionally Mara opened their conversation on her phone and studied the blank space beneath the latest message. Then she put the phone away.

***

When she returned from the archive, the bridge had displaced her monitor and one filing tray.

Mr. Venn stood beside it with two people from Procurement.

“We’ve identified a storage solution,” he announced.

“No,” Mara said.

All three looked at her.

Mara almost apologized.

Instead, she opened the ledger.

The Procurement people examined the drawings. One asked whether the archive contained a competitive quotation.

By six, everyone had gone home except Mara and the cleaner, who mopped around the growing structure without apparent surprise.

“Had one of those in my aunt’s garden,” the cleaner said.

“What happened?”

“My uncle crossed it.”

“And?”

“He came back with an apology.”

“Did it work?”

“The apology? Eventually.”

She wrung out her mop.

“Don’t stand under it when it gets bigger.”

At half past six, Mara called Tomas.

He answered on the fifth ring.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

A pause.

“Are you sure?”

“I wanted to ask you something.”

“All right.”

“Do you remember Mum’s kettle?”

The silence became so complete that she heard him breathing.

Then he said, “I’m not doing this tonight.”

The line went dead.

On the bridge, a second lamp came on.

***

Moving a bridge without authorization required a handcart, two loading ramps, and someone willing to hold a door.

Mr. Ilyan held the door.

The cleaner brought the ramps.

Mara pushed.

At the curb, the bridge slid off the handcart and settled onto the road with a sound like a heavy book being closed. Its arches rose. Its roadway lengthened. The seven lamps climbed until their glass lanterns hung above Mara’s head.

The eastern end stopped outside the bakery.

The western end stopped outside the cinema.

Between them, Bellwether Street bent downward into a space that had not been there a moment earlier.

It was not a hole. Mara could still see the white lane markings below. But the distance between the two pavements had become difficult to judge. The far side looked both thirty feet away and unreachable.

A cyclist braked.

“Roadworks?”

“Temporarily,” Mara said.

“How temporary?”

She checked her watch, though this was no help.

The cyclist dismounted and walked onto the bridge.

“Wait,” Mara called.

Halfway across, he stopped.

He stood with one foot on a pedal for nearly a minute. Then he turned around, came back, and took out his phone.

“Dad?” he said. “Have you got a moment?”

***

By morning, there were barriers.

By nine, there was a crowd.

By ten, a local news outlet had published a photograph under the headline **MYSTERY BRIDGE CAUSES PARKING CONFUSION**.

People crossed with mixed results.

A woman in a red coat reached the other side, sat on the pavement, and laughed until someone brought her water.

A delivery driver walked across twice and reported nothing except mild disappointment. On his third crossing, he remembered where he had put the spare key to his father’s house. He seemed pleased, though he would not explain why he had been looking for it.

Two schoolchildren ran across backward. One emerged carrying a conker. The other claimed to have heard the sea.

An elderly man approached the first arch, removed his hat, and went home without crossing.

The bridge did not charge admission or offer instructions.

Mara stayed beside the barriers with a clipboard, because holding a clipboard allowed her to remain close without being asked to leave.

At noon, a woman with silver hair came up beside her.

“The fourth light,” the woman said. “Still working?”

Mara recognized the voice.

“You sent it.”

The woman nodded.

“Why?”

“I was finished with it.”

***

Her name was Sera. She had once owned the cinema.

“My husband and I ran it for thirty-seven years,” she said. “After he died, I kept opening every evening. Even when nobody came.”

They sat on the bakery step.

A bus waited behind the bridge. Its driver had turned off the engine and was eating something from a paper bag.

“One night,” Sera continued, “I went upstairs to the projection room. There it was, between the projector and the wall. Small enough to step over.”

“What was on the other side?”

“A room in a house by the sea.”

“A real house?”

“It had a damp patch over the window. That seemed convincing.”

“Was your husband there?”

“No.”

Mara waited.

“I was rather angry about that,” Sera said. “But there was a bed made up, and something to eat in the kitchen. I stayed three days.”

“When you came back?”

“I still missed him. I also wanted to go somewhere else.”

She had sold the cinema, moved to a coastal town, and joined a choir despite possessing, by her own account, a voice like a cupboard being dragged.

“Why Bellwether Street?” Mara asked.

Sera pointed toward the dark cinema doors.

“It started there. I thought someone else nearby might need it.”

***

At two, Mr. Venn arrived with an engineer and a removal order.

The engineer tapped the stone, inspected the arches, and lowered a measuring tape over the side.

The tape descended twelve feet.

Then twenty.

Then forty.

The engineer wound it back up very carefully.

“I can’t certify this,” she said.

“Unsafe?” Mr. Venn asked.

“I didn’t say that.”

“Safe?”

“I didn’t say that either.”

Mr. Venn turned to Mara.

“It is blocking an adopted highway.”

“Yes.”

“It has no planning approval.”

“No.”

“We have received six complaints.”

“How many about the bridge?”

“Four. Two were about pigeons, but the timing suggests a connection.”

He handed her the order.

Mara looked toward the middle arch.

Five lamps were lit now.

“What happens when all seven come on?”

Sera, still sitting nearby, answered.

“It leaves.”

“With anyone on it?”

“No. Mine waited for me.”

Mr. Venn rubbed his forehead.

For the first time that day, Mara noticed how tired he looked.

“Give it until evening,” she said.

He looked at the engineer.

“I wouldn’t attach machinery to it,” the engineer said.

“Evening,” he conceded.

***

Tomas arrived just after five.

Mara saw him standing outside the pharmacy, hands in his coat pockets. He looked older than he did in photographs. So, presumably, did she.

“You said there was something I should see.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the bridge.

“Right.”

They stood together while a teenager crossed carrying a violin case.

On the other side, the teenager opened the case, took out the violin, and began tuning it.

“Is this some sort of apology?” Tomas asked.

“No,” Mara said.

His face closed.

“I mean, the bridge isn’t. I am.”

The violin produced a long, uncertain note.

Mara gripped the clipboard.

“I shouldn’t have thrown the kettle away.”

“It wasn’t about the kettle.”

“I know.”

“No,” he said. “You keep saying that, but I don’t think you do.”

She almost explained the hospital bills and the clearance deadline. She almost reminded him how little time they had and how much she had already done.

Instead, she asked, “What was it about?”

He stared across the street.

“Mum made tea when she didn’t know what to say. You remember? Bad exam results. Girlfriends. That time I crashed the van.”

Mara nodded.

“I wanted one thing from her kitchen,” he said. “Something I’d actually seen her hold.”

Mara put the clipboard down.

“I’m sorry.”

***

They crossed together.

For the first few steps, nothing happened.

Then the traffic quieted.

Mara smelled toast.

Halfway across, they found a kitchen. Its window stood open above the sink. Their mother’s blue apron hung from a hook, and the radio muttered beside a bowl of oranges.

There was no one in the room.

Tomas touched the back of a chair.

On the stove sat the yellow kettle.

Mara reached for it, then stopped.

“You take it.”

Tomas lifted it by the handle.

It was heavier than she remembered, with a brown stain around the spout and a loose lid that rattled when he moved.

They stayed until the light in the window began to fade.

Then they walked on.

On Bellwether Street, Tomas was empty-handed.

For a moment, he stared at his palm. Mara could not think of anything to say.

He rubbed his thumb against his fingers.

“Still warm,” he said.

The sixth lamp came on.

***

They bought tea from the bakery.

Tomas asked whether she still lived in the same flat. Mara asked about his work. Their answers were awkward and too detailed, full of things that would have been easier to mention years earlier.

At sunset, Mr. Venn returned.

He stopped beside the bridge and watched people crossing. Then, without removing his municipal identification badge, he walked over it himself.

When he came back, he sat down on the curb.

“Tomorrow,” he told Mara, “I’m taking annual leave.”

“How much?”

“I’ll let you know.”

The seventh lamp lit shortly after eight.

The bridge waited for a woman with a shopping trolley to reach the pavement. Then its lamps lowered, its arches folded inward, and Bellwether Street slowly became an ordinary street again.

Mara picked up the small stone bridge.

Tomas held open the envelope.

***

On Monday, Mr. Ilyan helped her establish a new archive category.

Mr. Venn, writing from an undisclosed holiday destination, approved it without requesting revisions.

The official designation was **Temporary Crossings for Unspecified Public Need**. Mara labeled the drawer **UNNECESSARY BRIDGES**, because otherwise people would keep asking her to prove necessity in advance.

The bridge stayed there for seven weeks.

Then, one rainy afternoon, she opened the drawer and found a little stone railway platform, complete with a clock and an empty bench.

She called the cleaner downstairs.

“Any thoughts?”

The cleaner examined it.

“Station Road, probably.”

“There’s already a station on Station Road.”

“Well,” said the cleaner, “perhaps it doesn’t go everywhere.”

Mara found a fresh form.

Under *reason for existing*, she began to write *transport*, then crossed it out.

She left the space blank and fetched the handcart.
